title: How Werewolves Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss werewolves: favorite werewolf movies (An American Werewolf in London, Teen Wolf, The Howling, Silver Bullet, The Wolf Man 1941, Twilight, True Blood), then folklore origins including the Epic of Gilgamesh, Ovid's Metamorphoses (Lycaon), lycanthropy as a term, voluntary wolf-skin transformations in Northern Europe, clothing and transformation symbolism, the transformation scene as a modern film convention (Rick Baker era), injuries carrying over after transformation, werewolf trials in 16th-17th century Europe including Gilles Garnier and Jean Grenier, explanations like ergot poisoning, hypertrichosis, rabies and wolf hybrids, the Beast of Gévaudan, hyena-men in Africa, Iberian godparent custom, and werewolves as sympathetic characters (Remus Lupin, Oz). Ends with listener mail from Kate about a guide dog named Kirrick in her fifth grade classroom.
topics: Iberian godparent custom seventh and ninth child

segments.title: Opening banter and favorite werewolf movies
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with talk of 'Werewolves of London' and their favorite werewolf films, including An American Werewolf in London, Teen Wolf, The Howling, and Silver Bullet, plus the 1941 Wolf Man.

segments.title: Werewolf movie rules and classic template
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the 1941 Wolf Man set the rules for werewolves: full moon transformation, silver bullet vulnerability, and incurability via bite, and note these became the iconic template.

segments.title: Ancient origins: Gilgamesh and Ovid
segments.summary: The earliest werewolf mention is in the Epic of Gilgamesh, where Ishtar turns a shepherd into a wolf. Ovid's Metamorphoses tells of Lycaon transformed by Jupiter, the source of the word lycanthropy.

segments.title: Shapeshifting folklore, voluntary transformation, and clothing
segments.summary: Shapeshifting fear is discussed, with varied folklore across cultures (hyenas in Africa, foxes in Japan). Voluntary wolf-skin transformations in Northern Europe and Iceland are covered, along with clothing's role in transformations and the werewolf as a symbol of leaving society.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A message break from the show's sponsor.

segments.title: Transformation scenes in modern film and injuries
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the detailed on-screen transformation became a modern film convention, contrasting with older literature and with Twilight and True Blood; they also note that injuries sustained as a wolf carry over to the human form.

segments.title: Werewolf trials and medical explanations
segments.summary: Werewolf trials in Europe between 1520 and 1630 are discussed, including self-confessed werewolves Gilles Garnier and Jean Grenier. Explanations include hallucinogens like ergot, hypertrichosis, rabies, and wolf hybrids. The Beast of Gévaudan is mentioned.

segments.title: Godparent custom and werewolves as sympathetic characters
segments.summary: The Iberian custom of older siblings acting as godparents for seventh and ninth children to ward off werewolves, practiced into the 1980s, is described. The hosts then discuss sympathetic werewolves in fiction such as Remus Lupin and Oz on Buffy.

segments.title: Closing and pointer to article
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the werewolf discussion and point listeners to the HowStuffWorks werewolf article.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kate's guide dog classmate
segments.summary: Kate writes about her fifth grade teacher Mrs. McKernan training a guide dog named Kirrick in the classroom. Kirrick did not pass final guide dog training but was adopted and later became a therapy dog.
